questions.text: Which of the following is true about cashless claim settlement?
options: The insured must always pay and claim later
Insurer directly pays approved bills to hospital or garage
questions.explanation: In cashless settlement, the insurer pays the claim amount directly to the hospital or service provider.

questions.text: The main purpose of reviewing insurance coverage periodically is to:
options: Ensure coverage remains adequate as life circumstances change
Get a refund of past premiums
questions.explanation: Reviewing coverage ensures the insured’s protection aligns with changing income, assets, and family needs.

questions.text: In the merchant ship example, the risk covered was:
options: Damage to goods carried by the ship
Loss of ship due to accident or storm
questions.explanation: The example illustrated insurance against the risk of a ship being lost at sea.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a requirement of an insurable risk?
questions.explanation: Speculative risks that involve the possibility of profit or gain are not insurable.

questions.text: Under-insurance implies:
options: The insured retains part of the risk
questions.explanation: Under-insurance means the coverage is less than the actual risk exposure, leaving part of the risk with the insured.

questions.text: The typical range of returns from traditional endowment policies is around:
questions.explanation: Traditional endowment policies typically yield about 3–5% per annum based on official illustrations.

questions.text: Which concept represents the present value of future income available to dependents?
questions.explanation: Human Life Value (HLV) is the present value of future income expected to support dependents.

questions.text: Which of the following cannot be covered under MWPA nominees?
questions.explanation: Under MWPA, only wife and/or children can be beneficiaries; parents are excluded.

questions.text: If a policyholder pays higher premium to get maturity value, the implied investment return can be found using:
options: Rate or XIRR function in Excel
questions.explanation: The internal rate of return on extra premium can be calculated using RATE or XIRR functions in Excel.

questions.text: A guaranteed bonus in life insurance is:
options: Fixed percentage of sum assured for initial policy years
questions.explanation: Guaranteed bonus is a fixed percentage declared for the first few years, forming part of contractual benefits.

questions.text: In the health vs critical illness comparison, health insurance is mainly suited for:
questions.explanation: Health insurance is meant to reimburse treatment costs; income replacement is better addressed via critical illness policies.

questions.text: Personal Accident insurance typically covers:
options: Death and specified disablements due to accident
Loss of job due to automation
questions.explanation: Personal Accident policies cover death, permanent total, permanent partial and temporary total disability from accidents.

questions.text: A general principle for global coverage of defined benefit policies (like life or accidental death) is that they:
options: Usually pay even if the insured event occurs outside India
Pay only if death occurs in India
questions.explanation: Defined benefit policies can usually be honoured globally as it is easier to verify the occurrence of the insured event.

questions.text: Critical illness insurance is best described as:
options: An indemnity policy that reimburses hospital bills
A defined benefit policy that pays lump sum on diagnosis of specified illnesses
A rider available only with motor policies
A compulsory cover under health plans
questions.explanation: Critical illness cover pays a fixed lump sum on diagnosis of listed illnesses, usually after a survival period.

questions.text: When claim amount is less than the sum insured of one chosen health policy, the insurer:
options: Must apply contribution from all policies
Cannot invoke contribution clause and must settle full admissible claim
Can pay only half the claim
questions.explanation: Contribution applies only when claim exceeds sum insured of the chosen policy; otherwise that insurer pays in full.

questions.text: The first step in the retirement planning process is to:
options: Estimate expenses and income required in retirement
questions.explanation: Planning begins with understanding what level of income is needed in retirement, which is based on expected expenses.

questions.text: During accumulation years, investors should prioritise:
options: Disciplined long-term investing with adequate insurance
questions.explanation: Long-term investing with protection from risk through insurance ensures corpus growth and security.

questions.text: Retirement planning has become more critical mainly because:
options: Life expectancy is increasing while formal benefits are shrinking
Gold is no longer a safe investment
questions.explanation: Longer life expectancy, rising costs, and shrinking formal retirement benefits make planning for post-retirement income essential.

questions.text: The corpus required for retirement depends primarily on:
options: Expected inflation, post-retirement returns, and longevity
questions.explanation: Inflation, longevity and post-retirement investment returns are the key inputs that determine corpus requirement.

questions.text: The ultimate goal of retirement planning is to:
options: Ensure financial independence and peace of mind during non-working years
questions.explanation: The real aim is long-term financial independence and a stress-free retired life with adequate income.

questions.text: Retirement expenses are generally NOT the same as pre-retirement expenses because:
options: Some expenses fall while others like medical and leisure may rise
Housing costs always disappear at retirement
questions.explanation: Loan EMIs, work-related costs may fall, but medical, travel and recreation often rise; tax may change as income changes.

questions.text: The typical risk-return hierarchy for retirement products places which highest on safety?
questions.explanation: EPF and PPF are government-backed and rank highest on safety among retirement products.

questions.text: Additional tax deduction of ₹50,000 for NPS contribution is available under:
questions.explanation: Section 80CCD(1B) provides an additional ₹50,000 deduction exclusively for NPS contributions.

questions.text: NPS Tier I account is:
options: Mandatory with tax benefits and withdrawal restrictions
questions.explanation: Tier I is the main retirement account under NPS; it is mandatory for government employees and enjoys tax benefits.

questions.text: PPF offers which tax treatment?
questions.explanation: PPF enjoys EEE status; contributions, interest, and withdrawals are all tax-exempt.

questions.text: The statutory contribution to EPF by employee and employer each is:
questions.explanation: Both employee and employer contribute 12% of the employee’s basic salary plus DA towards EPF.

questions.text: An employee becomes eligible for gratuity payment after:
questions.explanation: Employees completing at least 5 years of continuous service become eligible for gratuity.

questions.text: The primary role of an investment adviser in retirement planning is to:
options: Understand client goals and design strategies for steady post-retirement income
File tax returns on behalf of the client
questions.explanation: An investment adviser aligns client goals, risk tolerance, and timelines to ensure steady and sustainable post-retirement income.

questions.text: Transferring EPF balance to a new employer on job change is beneficial because:
options: It avoids taxation and retains continuity of service
questions.explanation: EPF transfer maintains service continuity, avoids tax, and ensures compounding benefits are preserved.

questions.text: The inflation-adjusted return on a retirement corpus earning 8% with 6% inflation is approximately:
questions.explanation: The real rate of return is calculated as (1+8%)/(1+6%) - 1 = 1.89%.

questions.text: Stepping up investments during accumulation years helps because:
options: It compensates for early low contributions and rising income
questions.explanation: Increasing contributions as income rises helps harness compounding and meet corpus goals efficiently.

questions.text: Philanthropy discussions help advisers:
options: Strengthen client relationships through value alignment
questions.explanation: Talking about values deepens trust and long-term adviser–client engagement.

questions.text: A key responsibility of an adviser while planning retirement income is to decide:
options: Client’s asset allocation and withdrawal rate
questions.explanation: Advisers determine sustainable withdrawal rates and design asset allocation to support income longevity.

questions.text: Long-term capital losses can be set off against:
questions.explanation: Long-term capital losses can only be set off against long-term capital gains.

questions.text: Assessment Year refers to:
options: The year in which income is earned
The year in which income is assessed and tax is paid
The year in which tax laws are enacted
questions.explanation: Assessment Year is the year following the previous year, in which income earned is assessed and taxed.

questions.text: Agricultural land in which area is NOT treated as a capital asset?
questions.explanation: Agricultural land situated in rural areas in India is excluded from the definition of capital asset.

questions.text: Long-term capital gains under the new regime are taxed at:
questions.explanation: Under the new provisions applicable from 23 July 2024, long-term capital gains are taxed at 12.5%.

questions.text: Gift of securities exceeding ₹50,000 without consideration is taxable under:
questions.explanation: Under Section 56(2)(x), gifts exceeding ₹50,000 in value are taxable under 'Income from Other Sources'.

questions.text: Which of these incomes is specifically included under 'Income from Other Sources'?
options: Winnings from lotteries or online games
questions.explanation: Winnings from lotteries, crossword puzzles, and online games are always taxed under 'Income from Other Sources'.

questions.text: For listed bonds, holding period to qualify as long-term capital asset is:
questions.explanation: Listed bonds qualify as long-term capital assets if held for more than 12 months.

questions.text: Under Chapter XII-A, long-term capital gains for NRIs are taxed at:
questions.explanation: NRIs opting for Chapter XII-A are taxed at 12.5% on long-term capital gains from eligible investments.

questions.text: Short-term capital gains on equity-oriented mutual funds are taxed at:
questions.explanation: Short-term gains on equity-oriented MFs with STT payment are taxed at 20%.

questions.text: Forfeiture of premium paid for share warrants results in:
questions.explanation: Forfeiture of warrant premium is ignored for tax computation; no deduction is allowed.

questions.text: Reverse mortgage loan proceeds are:
options: Taxable as income from other sources
questions.explanation: Loan amounts received under a notified reverse mortgage scheme are exempt under Section 10(43).

questions.text: Which of these transactions is NOT regarded as transfer under Section 47?
options: Conversion of preference shares into equity
questions.explanation: Conversion of preference shares into equity is explicitly excluded from transfer under Section 47(xb).

questions.text: When a person dies without a will, it is termed as:
questions.explanation: When no will exists, the person is said to have died intestate and property distribution follows succession laws.

questions.text: A 'codicil' refers to:
options: Supplement to a will altering its terms
questions.explanation: A codicil is an addition or alteration made to an existing will.

questions.text: When a will is destroyed intentionally by the testator, it results in:
questions.explanation: A will can be revoked by intentional destruction or by making a new one.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is true about a 'Registered Will'?
options: It provides stronger evidence of authenticity
It must be registered within 30 days
questions.explanation: A registered will is not mandatory but provides stronger legal proof of validity.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT an objective of estate planning?
options: Reducing income tax for business profits
questions.explanation: Estate planning focuses on asset transfer, not operational business tax reduction.

questions.text: Which of these statements is TRUE about a nominee?
options: Nominee is always the final heir
Nominee is merely a trustee of funds
questions.explanation: A nominee generally acts as a trustee for the legal heirs, unless designated as beneficial nominee.

questions.text: Who among the following can be appointed as a trustee?
questions.explanation: A trustee can be an individual or corporate entity capable of managing assets.

questions.text: A natural guardian is automatically assigned to:
questions.explanation: Parents are natural guardians of their minor children.

questions.text: Which Act defines the term 'Will' in India?
questions.explanation: Section 2(h) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 defines a Will.

questions.text: Which of the following Wills is valid even if not in writing?
questions.explanation: Privileged Wills can be oral, typically used by soldiers or mariners during warfare.

questions.text: Which Act governs Power of Attorney in India?
questions.explanation: POA is governed by both the Power of Attorney Act, 1882 and Contract Act, 1872.

questions.text: Which section of Income Tax Act exempts capital gains on transfer to an irrevocable trust?
questions.explanation: Transfers under an irrevocable trust are exempt under Section 47(iii).

questions.text: Which is NOT a common factor contributing to bubbles?
questions.explanation: Short-selling restrictions often worsen bubbles; widespread shorting would counteract them.

questions.text: Who introduced the concept of Bounded Rationality?
questions.explanation: Herbert Simon proposed Bounded Rationality, explaining how limited information leads to satisficing decisions.

questions.text: Overconfidence and self-attribution biases often lead investors to:
questions.explanation: Overconfidence combined with self-attribution leads to overtrading and poor diversification.

questions.text: Rebalancing portfolios when markets rise or fall helps:
options: Lock profits and manage risk systematically
questions.explanation: Rebalancing helps investors systematically take profits and control risk, avoiding emotional reactions.

questions.text: Chasing past performance means:
options: Investing based on historical returns expecting them to continue
questions.explanation: Chasing past performance assumes that last year’s winners will continue to perform, ignoring market cycles.

questions.text: Home country bias leads investors to:
options: Prefer domestic securities due to familiarity
Rely on foreign funds for safety
questions.explanation: Investors tend to invest only in their home country due to comfort and familiarity, missing global diversification benefits.

questions.text: SEBI requires that a client’s risk profile must be:
options: Updated periodically or after major life changes
questions.explanation: Regulations mandate regular review, especially after life or financial changes, to ensure suitability.

questions.text: Which of the following factors increases risk appetite?
questions.explanation: With more earning members, income stability improves, leading to higher risk tolerance.

questions.text: Risk profiling involves assessing which three factors?
options: Ability, Willingness, and Need to take risk
Tax rate, Portfolio value, and Tenure
questions.explanation: Risk profiling considers ability (financial capacity), willingness (psychological comfort), and need (goal requirement).

questions.text: A model portfolio helps advisers by:
options: Providing identical portfolios to all clients
Customizing recommendations based on client profile
questions.explanation: Model portfolios act as templates that can be customized based on each client’s unique circumstances.

questions.text: Moderate investors generally:
options: Understand risk is necessary for long-term goals
questions.explanation: Moderate investors balance risk and return and understand that some risk is essential for long-term wealth.

questions.text: Aggressive investors are most likely to:
options: Take active exposure to equities and growth assets
questions.explanation: Aggressive investors are experienced and willing to accept higher volatility for long-term gains.

questions.text: Strategic allocation is reviewed primarily when:
questions.explanation: Strategic allocation is long-term and revised mainly when fundamental changes occur in investor profile.

questions.text: Dynamic Asset Allocation uses:
options: Pre-defined models and valuation triggers for automatic rebalancing
questions.explanation: Dynamic asset allocation relies on pre-set models or valuation metrics to trigger portfolio rebalancing.

questions.text: Asset allocation primarily aims to:
questions.explanation: Asset allocation spreads risk across asset classes to stabilize returns and minimize loss exposure.

questions.text: Which personality trait is most associated with high risk-taking ability?
questions.explanation: Daring and adventurous individuals are psychologically more open to investment risks.

questions.text: What is the primary limitation of self-assessment risk profiling tools?
options: Investors may guess socially desirable answers
questions.explanation: Investors may attempt to 'guess' the right answers instead of responding truthfully, reducing accuracy.

questions.text: A valid risk profiling questionnaire should be:
questions.explanation: SEBI mandates that questionnaires should be simple, objective, and unbiased to ensure reliability.

questions.text: An investor near retirement should ideally have:
options: Balanced mix with higher debt allocation
questions.explanation: Retirees prioritize safety and income stability, so debt-heavy portfolios suit them better.

questions.text: In the coin toss example, the difference in people's decisions highlights:
questions.explanation: The example illustrates how individuals differ in their risk appetite despite similar expected returns.

questions.text: Fixed Maturity Plans (FMPs) are similar to:
questions.explanation: FMPs are closed-ended debt mutual funds with fixed tenure, often compared to FDs.

questions.text: Which form of gold investment does NOT attract GST?
questions.explanation: Sovereign Gold Bonds are paper-based and exempt from GST.

questions.text: In National Pension System (NPS) Tier 1, what percentage of corpus can be withdrawn tax-free at age 60?
questions.explanation: At retirement, 60% of NPS corpus can be withdrawn tax-free; 40% must be used to buy an annuity.

questions.text: Which product among the following provides guaranteed returns?
questions.explanation: PPF offers government-backed guaranteed returns that vary quarterly with G-sec yields.

questions.text: Category III Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) require a minimum investment of:
questions.explanation: AIF Category III has a minimum entry threshold of ₹1 crore per investor.

questions.text: Which of the following offers exposure to infrastructure assets?
questions.explanation: Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) invest in infrastructure projects like roads, ports, and power plants.

questions.text: Mutual Funds are regulated by ______, while ULIPs are regulated by ______.
questions.explanation: Mutual funds fall under SEBI, while ULIPs are under the jurisdiction of IRDAI.

questions.text: Between Company Deposits and Debentures, which is riskier?
questions.explanation: Company deposits are unsecured, whereas debentures are usually secured; hence deposits carry higher risk.

questions.text: REITs primarily invest in:
options: Infrastructure projects like bridges and roads
Commercial real estate generating rental income
questions.explanation: REITs (Real Estate Investment Trusts) mainly invest in income-generating commercial properties.

questions.text: Minimum investment amount for a Portfolio Management Service (PMS) is:
questions.explanation: As per SEBI norms, the minimum investment in PMS is ₹50 lakh.

questions.text: In comparison of debt instruments, liquidity is highest in:
questions.explanation: Bank FDs offer instant liquidity, albeit with penalties for premature withdrawal.

questions.text: Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs) differ from Index Funds because:
options: They are sold only by AMCs
They are traded on stock exchanges like shares
They are only available for debt instruments
questions.explanation: ETFs are listed and traded on exchanges, unlike index funds which are transacted at NAV with AMCs.

questions.text: ULIPs issued after February 1, 2021 lose Section 10(10D) exemption if annual premium exceeds:
questions.explanation: ULIPs with premiums above ₹2.5 lakh per year no longer qualify for tax exemption under Section 10(10D).

questions.case_text: Mr. and Mrs. Iyer, aged 67 and 63, live in their own house worth about ₹1.8 crore in a metro city. Their financial investments total only ₹18 lakh and they receive a small pension of ₹20,000 per month. Their monthly expenses are around ₹60,000. They are considering using a reverse mortgage loan on their house to supplement income, instead of selling the property. They want to understand how reverse mortgage works and its pros and cons.

questions.text: Reverse mortgage loans are primarily designed to:
options: Allow senior citizens to unlock home equity for regular income while continuing to live in the house
questions.explanation: Reverse mortgage enables elderly homeowners to receive periodic payouts or a lump sum by mortgaging their self-occupied home, without having to sell or vacate it, thereby converting illiquid home equity into usable cash flows.

questions.text: Which of the following is TRUE about OWNERSHIP during reverse mortgage?
options: Ownership immediately passes to the bank
Borrower must vacate the house within 1 year
Borrower retains ownership and occupancy rights during the loan tenure, subject to terms
The house must be rented out compulsorily
questions.explanation: The borrower continues to own and occupy the property during the term. The lender has a charge on the property and recovers dues when the loan terminates or on death, usually from sale proceeds.

questions.text: What typically happens when both Mr. and Mrs. Iyer pass away and reverse mortgage is in force?
options: Bank automatically becomes owner without any option to heirs
Heirs can repay the loan and redeem the house, or else the lender sells the property and returns any surplus after settling dues
questions.explanation: Heirs usually have the option to settle the outstanding loan and keep the property. If they do not, the lender can sell the house to recover dues and pay any balance to the legal heirs.

questions.text: Which is a KEY ADVANTAGE of reverse mortgage for the Iyers compared to selling the house outright?
options: Ability to continue living in the same house while generating income from home equity
No need to pay property taxes
questions.explanation: Reverse mortgage lets them monetize the property gradually without moving out. It is beneficial especially when emotional attachment to the home and desire for stability are high.

questions.text: Which factor should the Iyers consider BEFORE opting for reverse mortgage?
options: Views and needs of potential heirs, their own longevity and alternative income sources
Ability to get another home loan
questions.explanation: Reverse mortgage affects the eventual inheritance and long-term family plans. The Iyers must weigh their current income needs against heirs’ expectations, property market outlook and any emotional considerations about bequeathing the house.

questions.case_text: A retired couple, Mr. and Mrs. Rao (65 and 62), live on pension and interest income. They have health insurance of ₹3 lakh each with a co-pay clause of 20% after age 60. Mr. Rao undergoes a surgery costing ₹5 lakh. They are surprised to find that they still have to pay a significant amount from their pocket.

questions.text: If Mr. Rao’s health policy sum insured is ₹3 lakh with 20% co-pay on the claim amount, what will the insurer pay on a ₹5 lakh bill (assuming no other limits)?
questions.explanation: Co-pay of 20% on ₹5 lakh means insured bears ₹1 lakh. Insurer pays up to sum insured, but here 5 lakh – 1 lakh = 4 lakh; limited to ₹3 lakh sum insured, so effectively ₹3 lakh. However the question assumes co-pay on reimbursable amount within SI: 80% of 3 lakh = ₹2.4 lakh (closest structured exam-style interpretation).

questions.text: What is the PRIMARY purpose of a CO-PAY clause for insurers?
options: To share costs with insured and reduce small or unnecessary claims
questions.explanation: Co-pay requires the insured to bear part of the cost, discouraging overutilization and reducing claim outgo for the insurer.

questions.text: Which is a better approach for retirees like the Raos?
options: Lower sum insured with high co-pay
Higher sum insured with minimal co-pay even if premium is slightly higher
questions.explanation: At older ages, medical costs are high and frequent, so a higher sum insured with lower co-pay protects their retirement corpus.

questions.text: What is a key risk of under-insuring health expenses in retirement?
options: Erosion of retirement corpus due to medical shocks
questions.explanation: Large out-of-pocket medical costs can rapidly deplete savings earmarked for regular retirement living expenses.

questions.text: Which action would have helped reduce the Raos’ out-of-pocket burden?
options: Buying higher sum insured or super top-up cover earlier
Avoiding medical tests while buying the policy
questions.explanation: Increasing cover or adding top-up when they were younger and healthier would have been cheaper and provided better protection in retirement.

questions.case_text: Mr. Mehta, 70, has two children. He owns a self-occupied house, some mutual fund investments and bank deposits. He has written a Will, leaving the house to his son and financial assets to his daughter. He wants to ensure that his estate passes smoothly to his heirs and is concerned about disputes and delays.

questions.text: Which document primarily governs distribution of Mr. Mehta’s assets after his death?
questions.explanation: A valid Will is the legal document expressing how his estate should be distributed after death, subject to laws of succession.

questions.text: What is one ADVANTAGE of REGISTERING a Will?
options: Registration provides additional evidentiary value and reduces risk of tampering
Registration exempts all assets from tax
questions.explanation: Registered Wills are kept with the registrar, reducing chances of loss or forgery and strengthening evidentiary value.

questions.text: If Mr. Mehta dies without leaving a valid Will, the succession will be governed by:
questions.explanation: In absence of a Will, the estate devolves as per personal laws (Hindu Succession Act, etc.) relating to intestate succession.

questions.text: Which person is responsible for administering the estate as per the Will?
questions.explanation: The testator appoints an executor in the Will to carry out its instructions and distribute assets accordingly.

questions.text: To reduce the risk of disputes, Mr. Mehta should:
options: Keep his Will completely secret without clarity
Clearly communicate intentions to family and ensure Will is unambiguous
questions.explanation: Clear drafting, unambiguous bequests and open communication often reduce misunderstandings and legal disputes.

questions.case_text: A group of investors in an office WhatsApp group buy the same hot IPO because everyone is talking about it. Very few of them read the prospectus or research the company’s fundamentals. They are convinced that it will list at a huge premium because ‘everyone is applying’.

questions.text: Their behaviour of investing based on the crowd’s enthusiasm is an example of:
questions.explanation: Herd behaviour occurs when investors follow the actions of a larger group instead of independent analysis.

questions.text: Believing that the IPO will list at a premium merely because there is high demand reflects:
questions.explanation: They are extrapolating from recent ‘hot IPO’ stories and high subscription figures without deeper study.

questions.text: Which is a prudent step for an investor before applying to IPOs?
options: Study the DRHP/prospectus and understand business, valuations and risks
questions.explanation: Responsible investing requires understanding the company’s financials, use of proceeds, risks and pricing.

questions.text: If the IPO lists below issue price, many investors may refuse to sell and say ‘I will sell when I get back my cost’. This reflects:
options: Loss aversion and anchoring to purchase price
questions.explanation: They anchor to their purchase price and avoid realizing losses, even if fundamentals do not justify holding.

questions.text: How can a financial adviser reduce such behaviour?
options: By educating clients about valuation, risks and long-term investing discipline
questions.explanation: Advisers should promote evidence-based investing rather than emotional or herd-based decisions.

questions.case_text: Rohan, 38, is returning to India after working abroad for 10 years. He has accumulated foreign currency deposits, a 401(k)-type retirement account overseas, and mutual funds in India invested as an NRI. He plans to settle in India permanently with his spouse and two young children. He wants a comprehensive plan covering residential status, tax, asset allocation, and long-term goals such as children’s education and retirement.

questions.text: On returning permanently, Rohan’s RESIDENTIAL status for Indian tax purposes will depend on:
options: Number of days stayed in India in the relevant previous year and preceding years
questions.explanation: Indian tax residency is determined primarily by physical presence as per Income-tax Act rules, not by citizenship or account type. Day-count tests decide whether he becomes resident, resident but not ordinarily resident, or NRI.

questions.text: Why is it important to review his OVERSEAS retirement accounts and investments?
options: To understand tax implications, withdrawal rules and currency risks as he shifts his base to India
questions.explanation: Different countries have their own tax rules and penalties for withdrawals. Rohan must plan the timing and method of accessing these funds and consider currency risk relative to his rupee-based expenses.

questions.text: His NRI investments in Indian mutual funds and NRE deposits need to be reviewed because:
options: They may have to be redesignated as resident accounts when his status changes
questions.explanation: On change of residential status, bank and investment accounts must be updated (e.g., NRE to resident or RFC) to comply with FEMA and banking regulations. This may affect tax treatment and repatriation.

questions.text: For long-term goals in India, his asset allocation should primarily be:
options: Balanced across rupee assets like equity, debt and real estate aligned to goals and risk profile
questions.explanation: Since his future expenses (education, retirement) will be largely in rupees, the core of his portfolio should be in Indian assets suited to his goals and risk capacity, with any foreign exposure used thoughtfully for diversification.

questions.text: What is the FINANCIAL PLANNER’s key role in this situation?
options: Coordinating a holistic plan covering tax, FEMA compliance, risk management and investment strategy in consultation with specialists
questions.explanation: The planner provides an integrated roadmap, while working with tax and legal experts in both jurisdictions to ensure compliance, optimization and alignment with the family’s life goals.

questions.case_text: Ritesh (33) is considering a Unit Linked Insurance Plan (ULIP) pitched by an agent as a “two-in-one” product giving both insurance and investment. The ULIP offers life cover of ₹10 lakh with an annual premium of ₹1,20,000 for 20 years. Alternatively, a term plan for the same sum assured costs only ₹8,000 per year, and he could invest the balance premium into equity mutual funds. Ritesh wants to compare these options from a risk and wealth-creation perspective.

questions.text: How much PREMIUM per year would Ritesh SAVE if he chooses term insurance (₹8,000) instead of ULIP (₹1,20,000), assuming same sum assured?
questions.explanation: Annual premium saving = 1,20,000 (ULIP) – 8,000 (term) = ₹1,12,000. This excess can potentially be invested in pure investment products like mutual funds.

questions.text: From a pure RISK COVER perspective, which of the following is TRUE if the sum assured is the same (₹10 lakh)?
options: ULIP provides better risk cover than term plan
Term plan provides the same risk cover at much lower cost
Both ULIP and term plan have identical costs
ULIP offers risk cover only after 10 years
questions.explanation: A term plan provides the same mortality cover at a fraction of the premium because it does not bundle investment features. ULIP charges include mortality, fund management and various policy charges, making it costlier for the same insurance cover.

questions.text: If Ritesh chooses TERM + MUTUAL FUNDS route, where could the INVESTMENT portion (₹1,12,000 p.a.) be placed for long-term wealth creation aligned with his risk profile?
options: Equity-oriented mutual funds with suitable asset allocation
questions.explanation: Equity-oriented mutual funds, selected as per risk profile and goal horizon, provide transparent market-based growth and flexibility that is comparable or superior to ULIP fund options, but with greater cost efficiency and liquidity.

questions.text: Which aspect of ULIPs often reduces their attractiveness for short- to medium-term investors?
options: Very low charges in early years
5-year lock-in and high surrender penalties in early years
Guaranteed returns irrespective of market performance
questions.explanation: ULIPs generally have a minimum 5-year lock-in and may impose high surrender or discontinuance charges in initial years. This makes them unsuitable for investors who need flexibility or might exit early.

questions.text: From a FINANCIAL PLANNING perspective, which strategy is MOST appropriate for Ritesh?
options: High-premium ULIP as main savings product
Separate term insurance for protection and mutual funds for investment
No life insurance at all and only PPF
Only bank FDs with no insurance
questions.explanation: Separating protection (term plan) from investment (mutual funds) improves transparency, cost efficiency, and flexibility. It allows Ritesh to adjust his investment portfolio without disturbing his life cover.
